kurals.tamil:
வகையறிந்து வல்லவை வாய்சோரார் சொல்லின்
தொகையறிந்த தூய்மை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vakaiyarindhu vallavai vaaisoraar sollin
Thokaiyarindha thooimai yavar.
kurals.meaning: People of pure mind who know the full range of words, and who first size up what kind of assembly they are facing, will not stumble in their speech before a powerful gathering.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you know every line of the school play, and you have peeked out to see who is in the audience. Because you know your words and you know who is listening, your voice stays steady. Knowing your words and knowing your listeners keeps you from getting tongue-tied.
kurals.university: This couplet opens Avaiyañcāmai (“not fearing the assembly”). It pairs with the chapter before it, Avaiyaṟital (knowing the assembly), inside the Amaicciyal, the section on ministers. Parimelazhagar reads vakai aṟintu (“knowing the kind”) as first working out what sort of assembly one is in. Vallavai is the assembly of the able or powerful, and vāy sōrār means “their mouths will not slip,” that is, they will not falter or make mistakes out of fear. Sollin tokai aṟinda tūymaiyavar are “the pure who know the tokai (range or classification) of words,” which commentators connect with a grammarian’s knowledge of word-classes and how to use them. So the chapter’s first answer to stage fright is skill combined with integrity. The sandhi-joined text reads “சொல்லின் றொகையறிந்த,” where றொ is simply ன் fused with தொ, and the words are unchanged.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking truthfully and beneficially and in avoiding speech that offends. One should also recite the Vedas regularly.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a discipline of speech: words should be true and helpful, should not wound, and should rest on steady study of scripture.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita joins pure speech to learning in the same way the Kural praises “the pure who know the range of words.”
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: It pairs pure speech with study as the Kural does, but it says nothing about fear of an audience.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to speak graciously and with some bite, so that they can give each person a fitting answer.
christianity.tie_back: Knowing how to answer “every man” is close to the Kural’s knowing what kind of assembly one faces.
christianity._accuracy_note: The verse is about fitting one’s speech to each listener. Fear of the assembly is only implied.

islam.quote_or_event: “My Lord, expand for me my breast [with assurance] … And untie the knot from my tongue / That they may understand my speech.”
islam.explanation: Before facing Pharaoh’s court, Moses asks God to give him confidence and to free his tongue so that his words will be understood.
islam.tie_back: This is a prayer for exactly what the Kural describes: not stumbling in speech before a powerful gathering.
islam._accuracy_note: A strong match on steady, understandable speech before power. The Qur’an credits God as the source of that confidence, where the Kural credits learning and purity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise man does not speak before one who is greater than he in wisdom, And does not break into his fellow’s speech; And is not hasty to answer; He asks what is relevant, and he answers to the point”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah lists the traits of a wise person in discussion: he respects rank, does not interrupt, does not rush, and speaks to the point.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that well-ordered speech in learned company depends on knowing the setting and knowing how words work.
judaism._accuracy_note: It overlaps with the Kural on skilled, well-placed speech among scholars. It is about good manners rather than fear.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The Realized One knows the right time to speak so as to explain what he knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, but which is disliked by others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha sorts speech by whether it is true, whether it helps, and whether it is welcome. He speaks only what is true and beneficial, and he chooses the right moment.
buddhism.tie_back: This amounts to knowing the kinds of words and the kind of occasion, which the Kural says keeps a speaker from faltering.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarājakumāra Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: It closely matches the idea of classifying speech and timing it well, but it does not address fear of an audience.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says the Muses pour sweet dew on the tongue of a king they favour. His words then flow gently, he speaks surely in the assembly, and he quickly settles even a great quarrel.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod’s picture, a ruler who speaks well in public has been given the gift of the Muses, and the people look to him when he gives judgement.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Speaking steadily and without error before an assembly is the ideal the Kural describes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The two agree on assured public speech. Hesiod credits divine gift where the Kural credits learning and purity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that a true orator must know the different kinds of souls and the kinds of speech that suit each one, and must be able to see, in the moment, what sort of listener is in front of him.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the art of speaking rests on classifying both listeners and speeches and matching one to the other.
philosophy.tie_back: This is very close to vakai aṟintu, knowing the kind of assembly, joined with knowing the classes of words.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A close structural parallel. Plato stresses method more than courage.

kurals.tamil:
கற்றாருள் கற்றார் எனப்படுவர் கற்றார்முன்
கற்ற செலச்சொல்லு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Katraarul katraar enappaduvar katraarmun
Katra selachchollu vaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who can set out what they have learned before learned people, in a way that actually reaches them, are called the most learned of the learned.
kurals.elementary: Lots of kids can read a book. The one who can explain it clearly to the whole class, even with the teacher listening, is the one everyone calls the real expert.
kurals.university: The line repeats kaṟṟār (“the learned”) four times. The word-play mirrors the idea that learning is measured among the learned. The key term is cela-c-colluvār, “those who speak so that it goes (cel-)” into the hearers. Parimelazhagar glosses it as speaking so that the matter enters the listeners’ minds, and Mu. Varadarasanar likewise says “so that it settles in their hearts.” The judgement is about rank: standing among scholars comes from being able to explain things well before one’s peers, not from private learning. The sandhi-joined text reads “கற்றாருட் கற்றா ரெனப்படுவர் கற்றார்முற்,” in which ட் and ற் are sound-changes of ள் and ன் before க.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Janaka offers a thousand cows, with gold on their horns, to the most learned Brahmin at his sacrifice. When the others hesitate, Yajnavalkya claims the cows and then answers one questioner after another from the assembled scholars, including Gargi.
hinduism.explanation: Yajnavalkya’s standing as the foremost knower is settled in public, by answering the learned in front of the learned.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s “most learned of the learned” shown as an actual event.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.1-3.9 (trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A very close match. Rank among scholars is decided by answering before scholars.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.”
christianity.explanation: The twelve-year-old Jesus sits among the teachers of the Law, listening, asking and answering, and they are amazed.
christianity.tie_back: A young learner speaks before the learned and is recognised as learned himself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on speaking well before scholars. Luke emphasises understanding, not courage.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘O Adam, inform them of their names.’ And when he had informed them of their names, He said, ‘Did I not tell you that I know the unseen [aspects] of the heavens and the earth?’”
islam.explanation: The angels have admitted that they know only what they were taught. Adam, who has been taught the names of things, then lays out that knowledge before them.
islam.tie_back: Knowledge proves its worth when it is set out before a learned assembly, here the angels.
islam._accuracy_note: The shape matches: knowledge is shown before knowers. But the point of the verse is God’s knowledge, not human rank.

judaism.quote_or_event: The sons of Bathyra, leaders in Jerusalem, could not recall whether the Passover offering overrides the Sabbath. Hillel, a newcomer from Babylonia, proved the answer before them by formal reasoning and tradition, and they appointed him their head (Nasi).
judaism.explanation: Hillel’s leadership was granted because he could lay out his learning convincingly before the learned.
judaism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s claim: those who can explain before scholars are ranked first among scholars.
judaism._accuracy_note: A strong narrative parallel. The Talmud then adds a humbling twist when Hillel himself forgets a law.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That monk who has control over his tongue, is moderate in speech, unassuming and who explains the Teaching in both letter and spirit — whatever he says is pleasing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises the monk who can expound the teaching accurately and pleasingly.
buddhism.tie_back: Its standard of excellence, explaining the teaching so that it is well received, matches the Kural’s cela-c-collutal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: It matches on skilled exposition. It does not mention a learned audience or fear.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “when he raised his voice, and the words came driving from his deep chest like winter snow before the wind, then there was none to touch him, and no man thought further of what he looked like.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antenor remembers Odysseus coming to Troy as an envoy. At first he stood stiff with his eyes on the ground, but once he began to speak no one could match him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus proved himself foremost by speaking before an assembly of Trojan elders.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A vivid match: an unimpressive-looking man proves supreme by speaking before elders.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Quintilian takes up Cato’s definition of the orator as “a good man skilled in speaking” (vir bonus dicendi peritus) and makes it the goal of his whole course of education.
philosophy.explanation: For Quintilian, the complete man of learning is the one who can bring his knowledge and character to bear in public speech.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats effective speech before an audience as the crown of learning.
philosophy._accuracy_note: The two ideals are close. Quintilian stresses moral character, which sits closer to 721’s ‘purity.’

kurals.tamil:
பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர்
அவையகத்து அஞ்சா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pakaiyakaththuch chaavaar eliyar ariyar
Avaiyakaththu anjaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: People willing to die in the midst of enemies are easy to find. People who stand in an assembly without fear are rare.
kurals.elementary: Lots of people are brave in a game or on the playground. Standing up in front of the whole school to say what you really think takes a different kind of courage, and fewer people have it.
kurals.university: The couplet is built as a sharp contrast: pakai-y-akattu (“inside the enemy ranks”) against avai-y-akattu (“inside the assembly”), and eḷiyar (“easy to find, many”) against ariyar (“rare”). Parimelazhagar takes the first group as warriors who throw themselves fearlessly among the enemy and die, and the second as those who are unafraid before the learned. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the first as “many in the world.” The couplet ranks civil courage above martial courage, a bold claim in a culture whose puṟam poetry celebrated heroic death. The sandhi-joined text “பகையகத்துச் சாவா ரெளிய ரரிய / ரவையகத் தஞ்சா தவர்” divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Draupadi is dragged into the Kuru assembly hall after the dice game and asks whether she was lawfully staked. The great warriors and elders present, men who would later die bravely at Kurukshetra, sit silent. Only the young Vikarna, and Vidura, speak up for her.
hinduism.explanation: Heroes who feared nothing on the battlefield could not bring themselves to speak for justice in the assembly.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in dramatic form: many will die in battle, few will speak without fear in council.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: An unusually direct parallel: brave warriors are silent in the council hall.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Brought before the high council, two fishermen speak so boldly that the learned rulers are astonished.
christianity.tie_back: Fearless speech before a council is rare enough to make the members marvel, just as the Kural says such speakers are rare.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on rare boldness before an assembly. Acts attributes it to their time with Jesus rather than to learning.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best fighting (jihad) in the path of Allah is (to speak) a word of justice to an oppressive ruler.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks speaking a just word to a tyrant above other kinds of striving, including armed struggle.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it places courageous speech before power above courage on the battlefield.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4344 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: A very close match in how it ranks spoken courage above martial courage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law; and if I perish, I perish.”
judaism.explanation: Esther decides to enter the Persian king’s court unsummoned, which could mean death, in order to plead for her people.
judaism.tie_back: Speaking before a throne asks more courage than the Kural’s easy battlefield death, and Esther finds it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Her courage is to speak in a royal court, not in a learned assembly. The spirit is the same.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Sariputta that there are eight kinds of assembly: nobles, brahmins, householders, ascetics, and four orders of gods. He recalls entering hundreds of assemblies of nobles, sitting and talking with them, and seeing no ground for fear or timidity to arise in him.
buddhism.explanation: Fearlessness in every kind of assembly (vesārajja, self-assurance) is listed among the Buddha’s marks of greatness.
buddhism.tie_back: Being fearless in the assembly is presented as rare and admirable, as the Kural says.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 12, Mahāsīhanāda Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on fearlessness in assemblies. There is no contrast with the battlefield.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Son of Tydeus, in war your prowess is beyond question, and in council you excel all who are of your own years”
greek_mythology.explanation: Agamemnon proposes to give up and sail home, and everyone sits silent until the young warrior Diomedes rises and rebukes the king. Old Nestor then praises him for being brave both in war and in council.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In a room of silent chieftains, Diomedes shows the rarer courage of the council.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Nestor praises both courages together. The surrounding silence of the other kings shows that council courage is the rarer of the two.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “forsook his post, cast away his arms, and ran away most disgracefully”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch says that Demosthenes, the boldest speaker in the Athenian assembly, fled from the battle of Chaeronea.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the Kural. Courage in council and courage in battle are separate virtues, and a person can have one without the other.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Demosthenes 20 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin)
philosophy._accuracy_note: It inverts the Kural’s case. It confirms the two courages are distinct, but here the council courage is the one present.

kurals.tamil:
கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லித் தாம்கற்ற
மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Katraarmun katra selachchollith thaamkatra
Mikkaarul mikka kolal.
kurals.meaning: Present what you have learned before the learned so that it reaches them, and then take from those who know more whatever goes beyond your own knowledge.
kurals.elementary: Share what you know in class. Then listen to the teacher and the older kids who know even more. Speaking up and listening both help you grow.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats the formula kaṟṟār mun kaṟṟa cela-c-colli from 722 and adds a second duty: mikkāruḷ mikka koḷal, “take the surplus from those who surpass you.” Parimelazhagar reads mikkār as those superior in learning and mikka as whatever their learning holds beyond one’s own. The ytamizh commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) agree. Speaking before the learned is therefore not a performance but one part of a cycle of learning: speak, be tested, learn more. The sandhi-joined text has “தாங்கற்ற” and “மிக்காருண்” for தாம்கற்ற and மிக்காருள்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized soul can impart knowledge unto you because he has seen the truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna to seek out those who know more and to learn from them through questions and service.
hinduism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s second half: take the greater knowledge from those who surpass you.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A good match for the ‘learn from the greater’ half. It lacks the ‘speak before the learned’ half.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.”
christianity.explanation: Apollos, eloquent and mighty in the scriptures, preached boldly. Priscilla and Aquila, who understood more, then taught him further.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s cycle almost step by step: speak boldly before the learned, then learn more from those who know more.
christianity._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one narrative match for both halves of the couplet.

islam.quote_or_event: “Moses said to him, ‘May I follow you on [the condition] that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?’”
islam.explanation: Moses, a prophet already rich in knowledge, asks al-Khidr, who has knowledge Moses lacks, to teach him.
islam.tie_back: The learned take from someone greater the knowledge that goes beyond their own, which is exactly mikkāruḷ mikka koḷal.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on learning from the one who surpasses. There is no public-speaking element.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, “Who is wise?” and answers that the wise person is one who learns from every person.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah defines wisdom as an openness to keep learning from others, especially from those who know more.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats continued learning from others as the sign of true learning.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit, although Ben Zoma says ‘every person,’ not only those who are greater.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada urges us to seek out wiser people who will correct us, and to treat them as a treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Taking correction and more knowledge from those who surpass us is the second half of the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: It matches the learning-from-the-wiser idea. It says nothing about speaking before an assembly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Telemachus tells Athena, who is disguised as Mentor, that he has no practice in careful speech and that a young man feels shy about questioning an elder. She answers that some things he will think of himself and a god will prompt the rest, and he goes to question old Nestor.
greek_mythology.explanation: A shy youth overcomes his fear in order to speak before, and learn from, a man far wiser than himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He speaks before the learned and draws out knowledge from the one who knows more, both halves of the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A close match that even includes the shyness the chapter warns against.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Told by the oracle that no one was wiser than he, Socrates went to politicians, poets and craftsmen who were reputed to be wise, and questioned them in order to test the claim and to learn from them.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates’ method is to lay out questions before those with a reputation for learning in the hope of gaining from them.
philosophy.tie_back: He speaks before the learned and looks to learn more from them, even though he often found them lacking.
philosophy._accuracy_note: The method matches but the outcome does not: Socrates rarely found anyone who actually knew more.

kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க அவையஞ்சா
மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatrin alavarindhu karka avaiyanjaa
Maatrang koduththar poruttu.
kurals.meaning: Study the proper method of reasoning, by the rules, so that you can give answers in an assembly without fear.
kurals.elementary: If you want to answer tricky questions without getting nervous, practise thinking things through step by step. When you know how to reason, a hard question doesn’t scare you.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar reads āṟṟin aḷavu aṟintu kaṟka as “learn, by the proper path (of grammar), the aḷavai-nūl,” that is, the science of pramāṇa (means of valid knowledge), or logic. Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases it as tarka śāstra, the logic of proofs, and Kalaignar as grammar together with logic. Māṟṟam koṭuttal means “giving a reply,” so the purpose of this study is avai añcā, not fearing the assembly, above all when being cross-questioned. Some modern readers take āṟṟin aḷavu more loosely as “the measure of one’s ability” or “the scope of the subject.” The sandhi text “ஆற்றின் னளவறிந்து” shows a metrical doubling, and the words are the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Nyaya Sutra opens by listing sixteen subjects whose knowledge leads to the highest good. They include the means of valid knowledge (pramana), the parts of a formal argument, discussion (vada), wrangling, cavil, fallacies, and the ‘points of defeat’ at which a debater loses.
hinduism.explanation: Indian logic was built largely as a discipline for winning and judging debates in learned assemblies.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the aḷavai (pramāṇa) learning that Parimelazhagar says one must master in order to answer fearlessly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: It matches the very discipline the traditional commentary names.

christianity.quote_or_event: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers to be prepared at any time to explain and defend their faith.
christianity.tie_back: Being ready to give a reasoned answer is the Kural’s māṟṟam koṭuttal.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on readiness to answer. It does not prescribe formal logic.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the believer to argue in the best way, which assumes skill in reasoning and debate.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats well-trained argument as the way to face opponents.
islam._accuracy_note: It shares the ideal of good argument but does not mention fear or the study of logic.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be diligent in the study of the Torah; And know how to answer an epicuros”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar tells students to study hard so that they can reply to a skeptic.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural almost word for word in purpose: study so that you can give an answer.
judaism._accuracy_note: A very close functional match: learning aimed at readiness to reply.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the same way, when astute aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics come to see me with a question already planned, the answer just strikes me on the spot.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares himself to a charioteer who knows every part of a chariot. Because his understanding is thorough, answers come to him at once, even to questions prepared in advance.
buddhism.tie_back: Thorough learning is what makes a ready, fearless reply possible, which is the Kural’s argument.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarājakumāra Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: A close match on mastery producing ready answers to learned questioners.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “You knew nothing neither of war nor of the arts whereby men make their mark in council, and he sent me with you to train you in all excellence of speech and action.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Phoenix reminds Achilles that he was sent to train him in speaking in council as well as in fighting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek heroes also had to be trained for the assembly, which is the kind of preparation the Kural recommends.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: It matches on deliberate training for council speech. Logic as such is not mentioned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his essay on studies, Bacon says that reading makes a full man, conference (discussion) makes a ready man, and writing makes an exact man.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon holds that practice in discussion is what makes a person quick and ready in reply.
philosophy.tie_back: Disciplined preparation is what produces a ready reply, as the Kural argues.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased because the exact wording could not be verified against a live source. The point is close.

kurals.tamil:
வாளொடென் வன்கண்ணர் அல்லார்க்கு நூலொடென்
நுண்ணவை அஞ்சு பவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaalodden vankannar allaarkku noolodden
Nunnavai anju pavarkku.
kurals.meaning: What use is a sword to someone without courage? What use are books to someone who is afraid of an assembly of sharp minds?
kurals.elementary: A shiny sword is no use to a knight who runs away. In the same way, knowing lots of facts doesn’t help if you’re too scared ever to say them.
kurals.university: Two parallel questions, vāḷoṭu eṉ (“what [has he] to do with a sword?”) and nūloṭu eṉ (“what with books?”), set weapons and learning side by side. Vaṉkaṇ, literally “hard eye,” means steady courage. Nuṇ-avai is an assembly of subtle, sharp minds. Solomon Pappaiah takes nūl specifically as books of logic, continuing from 725, while Kalaignar reads it broadly as learning in general. On all readings the logic is the same: just as a sword is useful only to the brave, learning is useful only to someone who can use it before the learned. Owning it without using it is the same as not owning it. The sandhi text reads “வன்கண்ண ரல்லார்க்கு நூலொடெ / னுண்ணவை யஞ்சு பவர்க்கு.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “My whole body is trembling, and my hair is standing on end. My bow Gāṇḍīva is slipping from my hand, and my skin is burning.”
hinduism.explanation: Overwhelmed by dread on the battlefield, Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, feels his famous bow slipping from his grasp.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s image made literal: the best weapon is useless in a hand that shakes with fear.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 1.29 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A vivid match for the sword half. Arjuna’s fear is moral anguish rather than ordinary cowardice.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the servant who buried his master’s money out of fear is condemned for letting it go unused.
christianity.tie_back: A gift left unused because of fear is worthless, just like books in the hands of someone who fears the assembly.
christianity._accuracy_note: A close parallel: fear leads to burying something valuable.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an likens people who carry scripture but do not act on it to a donkey loaded with books it cannot use.
islam.tie_back: Learning that is carried but never used is as useless as the books the Kural says a timid scholar owns.
islam._accuracy_note: The image of useless learning is exact. The verse is about failing to act on scripture, not about fear.

judaism.quote_or_event: When God calls him to be a prophet, Jeremiah protests that he cannot speak because he is only a youth. God tells him not to fear their faces, promises to be with him, and puts words in his mouth.
judaism.explanation: The prophet is given his message and still has to overcome his fear of audiences before the message can be of any use.
judaism.tie_back: The word without the courage to speak it goes unused, which is the Kural’s point.
judaism._accuracy_note: It shares the problem of fear blocking speech. The resolution is divine help, not human training.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A learned person doesn’t have the insecurities of a person of little learning.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists learning among the qualities that make a trainee self-assured rather than timid.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism holds that learning should remove timidity, so learning that leaves a person afraid has failed at its purpose.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.101, Sārajja Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: It supports the Kural from the opposite side: learning is meant to produce confidence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Alexandrus quailed as he saw Menelaus come forward, and shrank in fear of his life under cover of his men.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Paris, armed with bow, sword and two spears, shrinks back from Menelaus, and Hector scolds him as someone fair to look at but with neither wit nor courage.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the Kural’s man with a sword but without courage.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A direct illustration of the sword half of the couplet.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is absurd to hold that a man ought to be ashamed of being unable to defend himself with his limbs, but not of being unable to defend himself with speech and reason, when the use of rational speech is more distinctive of a human being than the use of his limbs.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that being unable to defend oneself in speech is at least as shameful as being unable to defend oneself physically.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, puts armed self-defence and verbal self-defence side by side and counts failure in either as shameful.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A remarkably close structural parallel between the two kinds of defence.

kurals.tamil:
பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள் அவையகத்து
அஞ்சு மவன்கற்ற நூல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pakaiyakaththup pedikai olvaal avaiyakaththu
Anju mavankatra nool.
kurals.meaning: The learning of someone who is afraid in the assembly is like a gleaming sword in the hand of a man unfit to fight, facing the enemy: sharp, but never used.
kurals.elementary: Picture a very sharp, shiny sword held by someone who is shaking too hard to lift it. It looks impressive but does nothing. Learning you’re too scared to share is just like that sword.
kurals.university: This couplet turns 726 into a single simile: pēṭi kai oḷ vāḷ, “the bright sword in the hand of a pēṭi.” In classical Tamil, pēṭi means a person who is neither man nor woman, traditionally glossed as a eunuch or hermaphrodite. Pope and Drew translate it “hermaphrodite,” and Pope’s verse has “sexless being.” The martial culture of the time used such a person as a stock figure for someone unfit for battle; the image reflects that period’s assumptions, not a judgement the modern reader needs to share. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all stress uselessness: the sword is fine, but the hand fails it. The couplet also repeats 723’s pakai-y-akattu / avai-y-akattu frame. The sandhi text reads “பேடிகை யொள்வா ளவையகத் / தஞ்சு மவன்கற்ற நூல்.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna rebukes Arjuna’s collapse with the word klaibya, the state of a klība, a man unfit for manly action, and tells him to stand up.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita uses the same kind of image as the Kural’s pēṭi, a warrior disarmed by fear, to shame a skilled man into using his skill.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: An unusually exact cultural parallel. Klība and pēṭi belong to the same imagery.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the garden of Gethsemane, Peter draws his sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant. Hours later, in the high priest’s courtyard, he denies knowing Jesus when a servant girl questions him.
christianity.explanation: Peter’s sword is quick, but his courage fails him the moment he has to speak before those around him.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pairing of sword and assembly, showing that a drawn blade is no proof of courage to speak.
christianity._accuracy_note: A suggestive narrative parallel. Peter’s failure is denial under questioning rather than scholarly timidity.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whoever turns his back to them on such a day, unless swerving [as a strategy] for war or joining [another] company, has certainly returned with anger [upon him] from Allah”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an condemns the fighter who flees the battle line out of fear.
islam.tie_back: An armed man who flees is the first half of the Kural’s simile.
islam._accuracy_note: It covers only the battlefield image and says nothing about learning.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What man is there that is fearful and faint-hearted? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren’s heart melt as his heart.”
judaism.explanation: Before battle, the Torah sends fearful soldiers home, because a frightened fighter is of no use and weakens everyone else.
judaism.tie_back: An armed but fearful man is useless, which is the core of the Kural’s simile.
judaism._accuracy_note: A close match for the image. The application to learning is left to the reader.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Firstly, one warrior falters and founders at the mere sight of a cloud of dust. He doesn’t stay firm, and fails to plunge into battle.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes five kinds of warrior, the first of whom loses his nerve before the fighting even starts, and compares them to monks who give up.
buddhism.tie_back: An armed man who falters before battle is exactly the pēṭi’s useless sword.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.75, Yodhājīva Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on the warrior image. The Buddha applies it to spiritual life rather than to learning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Hector challenges any Achaean champion to single combat, the Greek chiefs sit silent, ashamed to refuse and afraid to accept, until old Nestor shames them and nine warriors finally stand up.
greek_mythology.explanation: Fully armed heroes are frozen by fear until they are reproached.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Weapons in the hands of men gripped by fear are worth nothing until courage returns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A good illustration of armed men paralysed by fear. The fear is overcome quickly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus notes that a lyre player who sings and plays well on his own becomes anxious when he walks into the theatre. The cause is not a lack of skill but his wish for applause, which is not in his control.
philosophy.explanation: Fear of the audience, not lack of ability, is what makes a skilled performer falter.
philosophy.tie_back: The skill is sharp but unusable once the performer is afraid, like the gleaming sword in the Kural.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A close psychological parallel. Epictetus also offers a Stoic cure that the Kural does not.

kurals.tamil:
பல்லவை கற்றும் பயமிலரே நல்லவையுள்
நன்கு செலச்சொல்லா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pallavai katrum payamilare nallavaiyul
Nanku selachchollaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: However many subjects they have studied, people who cannot put good things well and persuasively before a good assembly are of no use.
kurals.elementary: A treasure chest that stays locked forever is no better than an empty box. If you learn lots of things but never share them clearly, nobody gets any good out of them.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on the syllable avai: pal-l-avai (“many things”) and nal-l-avai (“a good assembly”) echo each other. Payam ilar means “without benefit.” Here payam is the classical form of payaṉ (use, fruit), not the modern Tamil word for fear, a false friend worth pointing out in a chapter about fear. Nalla avai is the assembly of good or learned people, and naṉku cela-c-collutal again means speech that reaches and persuades (see 722). Solomon Pappaiah adds that such a person is useless to the world, extending the loss from the individual to society. The sandhi text reads “நல்லவையு / ணன்கு.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad pairs every duty with svādhyāya-pravacana, one’s own study together with teaching it to others. In the graduation address the teacher tells the departing student not to neglect study and teaching.
hinduism.explanation: In the Vedic ideal, learning is incomplete unless it is also passed on to others.
hinduism.tie_back: Learning that is never expounded falls short, which is why the Kural calls the silent scholar useless.
hinduism.source: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.9 and 1.11 (trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A close match on the duty to teach what one learns. It does not speak of assemblies or fear.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says light is meant to be seen; hiding it defeats its purpose.
christianity.tie_back: Hidden learning, like a covered lamp, benefits no one.
christianity._accuracy_note: A well-known image for the same point about unshared gifts.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who is asked something he knows and conceals it will have a bridle of fire put on him on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that withholding knowledge when asked is a serious fault.
islam.tie_back: Knowledge that is not conveyed fails its purpose, as the Kural says of the learned person who cannot speak.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 3658 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: It shares the point that knowledge must be passed on. The hadith condemns deliberate concealment, not inability.

judaism.quote_or_event: Moses tells God that he is slow of speech and slow of tongue. God answers by appointing Aaron as his spokesman, so that what Moses knows can reach the people.
judaism.explanation: Even Moses’ knowledge needed a voice before it could help anyone.
judaism.tie_back: Learning has to be spoken well in order to be of use, which is the Kural’s point.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the need to convey knowledge. Here the problem is solved by a spokesman rather than by the scholar’s own courage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that a great deal of textual learning brings no benefit if it is never put to use.
buddhism.tie_back: Learning much but gaining nothing from it is the Kural’s verdict on the scholar who cannot speak.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The Dhammapada’s ‘use’ is practice, where the Kural’s is public speech. Both say learning left unused is wasted.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the gods do not grace all men alike in speech, person, and understanding. One man may be of weak presence, but heaven has adorned this with such a good conversation that he charms every one who sees him; his honeyed moderation carries his hearers with him so that he is leader in all assemblies of his fellows”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus tells Euryalus, who is handsome but tactless, that real standing in the assembly comes from skill in speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Only those who can speak well lead in the assembly, and other gifts count for little without that skill.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Odysseus contrasts looks with speech, where the Kural contrasts learning with speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Isocrates, the most famous teacher of rhetoric in Athens, admits that he lacked a strong voice and the boldness needed to face crowds. So he never addressed the assembly himself and worked through written speeches and teaching instead.
philosophy.explanation: Here is a man of great learning who could not deliver it before the assembly in person.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a real case of the Kural’s learned man unable to speak in the assembly.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A genuine historical case. Unlike the Kural’s scholar, Isocrates made his learning useful through writing.

kurals.tamil:
கல்லா தவரின் கடையென்ப கற்றறிந்தும்
நல்லா ரவையஞ்சு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallaa thavarin kadaiyenba katrarindhum
Nallaa ravaiyanju vaar.
kurals.meaning: People who have studied and understood, yet dread an assembly of good people, are said to rank even lower than the unlearned.
kurals.elementary: If a kid knows the answer but stays quiet because they’re scared, it’s as if they never knew it. It might even be worse, because a kid who doesn’t know can at least ask a question.
kurals.university: Kaṭai means “the lowest,” so kallātavariṉ kaṭai is “lower than the unlearned.” The verb eṉpa (“they say”) presents the judgement as the verdict of the wise. Kaṟṟu aṟintum, “though they have learned and understood,” stresses both study and understanding, so the failure is purely a failure of nerve. Solomon Pappaiah reads avai añcuvār as those so afraid that they do not even go to the assembly. The ranking is harsh because the unlearned at least lack the means, while the learned coward wastes what he has. Variant: thirukkural-thamizh’s sandhi text reads “கல்லா தவரிற் கடையென்ப கற்றறிந்து / நல்லா ரவையஞ்சு வார்,” where the final -um of கற்றறிந்தும் is absorbed before ந; ytamizh prints the separated form கற்றறிந்தும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Vidura teaches that a gathering without elders is no true assembly, and that elders who do not speak for dharma are not true elders.
hinduism.explanation: Vidura says that seniority and learning lose their worth when their holders stay silent where justice needs to be spoken.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: learned people who fear the assembly fall below those who have no learning at all.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Vidura Niti (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit. The exact verse number varies between editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue: For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.”
christianity.explanation: Educated leaders who privately believed stayed silent in public out of fear of their peers.
christianity.tie_back: The learned who know the truth but fear the assembly are judged harshly, as in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: A close match: learned insiders silenced by fear of the assembly.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Allah praises] those who convey the messages of Allah and fear Him and do not fear anyone but Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who deliver what they have been given without fearing people.
islam.tie_back: Fear of people is what the Kural condemns in the learned.
islam._accuracy_note: The Qur’an praises the positive side. The Kural condemns the failure.

judaism.quote_or_event: Moses tells the judges of Israel not to be afraid of any man’s face when they give judgement, because judgement belongs to God.
judaism.explanation: Those entrusted with legal knowledge are commanded not to let fear of people silence or bend them.
judaism.tie_back: Learning betrayed by fear of the audience is exactly what the Kural condemns.
judaism._accuracy_note: The two share the ‘fear no face’ ethic, applied here to judges.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is not wise because one speaks much. He who is peaceable, friendly and fearless is called wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada includes fearlessness in its definition of the wise.
buddhism.tie_back: If wisdom includes fearlessness, a learned person ruled by fear falls short of it, as the Kural implies.
buddhism._accuracy_note: It supports the link between wisdom and fearlessness. It also warns against mere talkativeness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Young Telemachus calls the first assembly Ithaca has held in twenty years, takes the speaker’s staff, and openly confronts the suitors who are devouring his house, even though he breaks into tears at the end.
greek_mythology.explanation: An inexperienced youth forces himself to speak before the whole community.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the opposite of the Kural’s coward: someone who masters fear of the assembly despite his youth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A positive counterpart to the Kural rather than a direct parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “although he had a style of speaking which was most like that of Pericles, he was throwing himself away out of weakness and lack of courage, neither facing the multitude with boldness”
philosophy.explanation: After young Demosthenes was jeered in the assembly, the old man Eunomus scolded him for wasting real ability through timidity.
philosophy.tie_back: Talent and learning wasted by fear of the crowd is precisely the failing the Kural ranks below ignorance.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Demosthenes 6 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin)
philosophy._accuracy_note: A very close case: real ability thrown away through fear of the assembly.

kurals.tamil:
உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர் களன்அஞ்சிக்
கற்ற செலச்சொல்லா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulareninum illaarodu oppar kalananjik
Katra selachchollaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: People who fear the assembly and so cannot pass on what they have learned in a way that reaches the hearers are like the dead, even though they are alive.
kurals.elementary: A lamp that is never switched on might as well not be there. When fear stops you from ever sharing what you know, it is as if that part of you isn’t there at all.
kurals.university: Uḷar eṉiṉum (“though they exist, are alive”) and illārotu oppar (“they are equal to those who are not”) set being against non-being. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read illār as the dead. Kaḷaṉ (kaḷam, “arena, place of assembly”) stands in for avai for variety, and añci (“fearing”) names the cause. The closing phrase kaṟṟa cela-c-collātār repeats the formula of 722 and 724 and ties the chapter together: to learn but not to pass it on is a kind of death. The sandhi text reads “உளரெனினு மில்லாரொ டொப்பர் களனஞ்சிக்.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that shrinking from his duty out of fear would bring a disgrace worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: In the Gita as in the Kural, a failure of nerve leaves a man worse than dead.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Both give the same ‘worse than death’ verdict on fear. The Gita is about duty in battle, not speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ tells the church at Sardis that it has the reputation of being alive but is in fact dead.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Alive in name but dead in fact’ is almost the Kural’s own wording for the silent scholar.
christianity._accuracy_note: The verbal parallel is striking, but the context is spiritual lukewarmness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him light by which to walk among the people like one who is in darkness, never to emerge therefrom?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes someone given life and light to walk among people, in contrast with someone still in darkness.
islam.tie_back: Real life means bringing one’s light among people, and the Kural says those who cannot are like the dead.
islam._accuracy_note: The life-and-death imagery matches. The verse is about faith, not public speech.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jeremiah says that when he decided to stop speaking God’s word, it became like a fire shut up in his bones, and he grew weary of holding it in and could not.
judaism.explanation: For the prophet, keeping a message unspoken is a torment that eats him from inside.
judaism.tie_back: Knowledge held back instead of spoken makes life unbearable, which is close to the Kural’s ‘alive yet like the dead.’
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in feeling. Jeremiah’s silence comes from weariness under persecution rather than stage fright.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful die not. The heedless are as if dead already.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls the heedless as good as dead even while they live.
buddhism.tie_back: It uses the same ‘living yet dead’ judgement the Kural passes on the fearful scholar.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The imagery matches but the cause differs: heedlessness rather than fear of the assembly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After his quarrel with Agamemnon, Achilles sits by his ships and goes neither to the assembly, where men win glory, nor to war, and he lets his heart waste away.
greek_mythology.explanation: Cut off from both assembly and battle, the greatest hero lives on but wastes away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Withdrawing from the assembly is a slow death of the self, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Achilles withdraws out of anger, not fear, but the result is the same wasted life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that if wisdom were given to him on condition that he keep it shut up and never declare it, he would refuse it, because no good thing is pleasant to possess unless it can be shared.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, wisdom that can never be passed on is not worth having.
philosophy.tie_back: Learning that is never spoken counts for nothing, the same verdict as the Kural’s.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A close match in value judgement. Seneca speaks of sharing, not fear of assemblies.
